cor-basis-existence.title: Existence of Basis
cor-basis-existence.html: Every finite spanning set of a vector space V contains a basis.

def-additive-inverse-notation.title: Notation of Additive Inverse
def-additive-inverse-notation.html: The unique inverse of a vector v∈V, for a vector space V over F, will be denoted as −v.

def-basis.title: Basis
def-basis.html:
A subset B of a vector space V is called a basis for V if:

  1. B is linearly independent;
  2. B spans V.

def-coordinates.title: Coordinates
def-coordinates.html: Let B={v1,…,vn} be an ordered basis for V. For any v∈V, the unique scalars c1,…,cn such that v=∑civi are called the coordinates of v with respect to B. We write this as a column vector: [v]B=[c1c2⋮cn].

def-dimension.title: Dimension
def-dimension.html: A vector space V over F is called finite-dimensional if it has a finite basis. The dimension of V, denoted dimF⁡(V), is the number of vectors in any basis for V. By convention, dimF⁡({0})=0.

def-direct-sum.title: Direct Sum of Two Subspaces
def-direct-sum.html: Let W1, W2 be subspaces of a vector space V. If W1∩W2={0}, then we write W1+W2 as W1⊕W2 and call it the direct sum of W1 and W2.

def-linear-combination.title: Linear Combination
def-linear-combination.html: Let V be a vector space over F, S={v1,v2,…,vm} be a subset of V. Then the expression a1v1+a2v2+⋯+amvm is called a linear combination of S. The scalars ai are called the coefficients of the linear combination.

def-linear-independence.title: Linear Independence
def-linear-independence.html:
A subset S of a vector space V is said to be linearly independent if for any distinct vectors v1,v2,…,vn∈S, the only solution to the equation: a1v1+a2v2+⋯+anvn=0 is the trivial solution a1=a2=⋯=an=0.

If there exists a non-trivial solution (where at least one ai≠0), then S is said to be linearly dependent.

def-span.title: Span
def-span.html:
Let S be a subset of a vector space V over F. The span of S, denoted by spanF(S), is the set of all linear combinations of finite subsets of elements of S.

If S={v1,v2,…,vn}, then spanF(S)={a1v1+a2v2+⋯+anvn:ai∈F}. By convention, spanF(∅)={0}.

def-spanning-set.title: Spanning Set
def-spanning-set.html: If span(S)=V, we say that S spans V, or that S is a spanning set for V.

def-subspace.title: Subspace
def-subspace.html: Let V be a vector space over F. A subset W of V is called a subspace of V, if W is also a vector space over F with addition and scalar multiplication inherited from V.

def-sum-of-subspaces.title: Sum of Subspaces
def-sum-of-subspaces.html: Let W1, W2 be subspaces of a vector space V. Then we define W1+W2:={w1+w2:w1∈W1 and w2∈W2}.

def-vector-space.title: Vector Space
def-vector-space.html:
A set V over a field F with two operations: addition + and scalar multiplication ⋅ +:V×V→V,⋅:F×V→V such that satisfy the following axioms for all v1,v2,v3∈V and α,β∈F:

  1. v1+v2=v2+v1
  2. (v1+v2)+v3=v1+(v2+v3)
  3. There exists 0∈V such that v1+0=v1
  4. There exists v1′∈V such that v1+v1′=0
  5. α(v1+v2)=αv1+αv2
  6. (α+β)v1=αv1+βv1
  7. α(βv1)=(αβ)v1
  8. 1v1=v1

def-vectors-scalars.title: Vectors and Scalars
def-vectors-scalars.html:
Let V be a vector space over F. Then the elements of V are called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars.

Additionally, 0∈V is called the zero vector, and (v1′) in (VS4) is called the inverse element of v1.

eq-linear-combo.html: ∑i=1nαibi+∑j=1pβjsj+∑k=1qγktk=0

exm-differentiable-functions.title: Differentiable Functions
exm-differentiable-functions.html:
Let C(R)={f:R→R∣f is continuous} be the set of all continuous functions on R. We consider the set of differentiable functions: D(R)={f:R→R∣f is differentiable} To verify that D(R) is a subspace of C(R):

  • Subset: Since differentiability implies continuity, we have D(R)⊆C(R).
  • Zero vector: The zero function f(x)=0 is differentiable, so 0∈D(R).
  • Closure under addition: If f,g∈D(R), then f+g is differentiable with (f+g)′=f′+g′, so f+g∈D(R).
  • Closure under scalar multiplication: If f∈D(R) and c∈R, then cf is differentiable with (cf)′=cf′, so cf∈D(R).

Thus, D(R) is a subspace of C(R).

exm-dimensions.title: Examples of Dimensions
exm-dimensions.html: dim⁡(Fn)=n, dim⁡(F[x]≤n)=n+1, and dim⁡(Mm×n(F))=mn.

exm-direct-sum-of-matrix.html:
Consider the vector space V=Mn(C), and two of its subspaces:

  • W1={A∈Mn(C):A⊤=A} (the subspace of symmetric matrices);

  • W2={A∈Mn(C):A⊤=−A} (the subspace of skew-symmetric matrices).

We can derive that V=W1⊕W2.

Proof. We first show that V=W1+W2. That is, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix. Let A∈Mn(C), notice that we have the identity: A=12(A+A⊤)+12(A−A⊤) where the first term is symmetric and the second term is skew-symmetric. Therefore, any square matrix is a sum of a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix.

To establish that W1∩W2={O}, let A∈W1∩W2. By definition, this implies A∈W1 and A∈W2. Consequently, the identities A=A⊤ and A=−A⊤ must hold simultaneously. Substituting the former into the latter yields A=−A. This implies 2A=O, and thus A=O.

exm-line-not-subspace.title: Translated Line is Not a Subspace
exm-line-not-subspace.title_html: Translated Line is Not a Subspace
exm-line-not-subspace.html: W={(x,y)∈R2:x+2y=3} is not a subspace of R2. This is because it does not contain the zero vector: 0+2(0)=0≠3, so (0,0)∉W.

exm-line-subspace.title: Line as Subspace
exm-line-subspace.html:
W={(x,y)∈R2:x+2y=0} is a subspace of R2. Indeed:

  • Zero vector: (0,0)∈W since 0+2(0)=0.
  • Addition: If (x1,y1),(x2,y2)∈W, then (x1+x2)+2(y1+y2)=(x1+2y1)+(x2+2y2)=0+0=0, so their sum is in W.
  • Scalar multiplication: If (x,y)∈W and c∈R, then (cx)+2(cy)=c(x+2y)=c(0)=0, so c(x,y)∈W.

exm-linear-combinations.title: Examples of Linear Combinations
exm-linear-combinations.html:
Below are some examples of linear combinations in different vector spaces:

  1. The vector (2,1,0) in R3 is a linear combination of S={(1,2,3),(4,5,6)} because (2,1,0)=−2⋅(1,2,3)+1⋅(4,5,6).

  2. The polynomial f(x)=x3+2x+1 in R[x] is a linear combination of S={1,x,x2,x3} because f(x)=1⋅1+2⋅x+0⋅x2+1⋅x3.

exm-linear-independence.title: Examples of Linear Independence
exm-linear-independence.html:
The following examples illustrate how to check for linear independence in various settings:

  1. Let S1={(1,2,3),(4,5,6)}⊆R3. To check linear independence, suppose a(1,2,3)+b(4,5,6)=(0,0,0)⟹{a+4b=02a+5b=03a+6b=0 The first two equations give a=−4b and 2(−4b)+5b=0⟹−3b=0. Thus a=b=0, so S1 is linearly independent.

  2. Let S2={(1,2,3),(4,5,6),(7,8,9)}⊆R3. Note that (1,2,3)−2(4,5,6)+(7,8,9)=(1−8+7,2−10+8,3−12+9)=(0,0,0). Since there exists a non-trivial solution, S2 is linearly dependent.

  3. Consider {2x+1,x2+3} in R[x]≤2. Suppose a(2x+1)+b(x2+3)=0⟹bx2+2ax+(a+3b)=0. Comparing coefficients of x2,x,1, we have b=0, 2a=0, and a+3b=0. This implies a=b=0, so the set is linearly independent.

  4. Consider {sin⁡x,cos⁡x,ex} in D(R). Suppose for all x∈R: asin⁡x+bcos⁡x+cex=0. Setting x=0 gives b+c=0. Setting x=π gives −b+ceπ=0. Adding these gives c(1+eπ)=0, so c=0 and hence b=0. Finally, setting x=π/2 gives a+ceπ/2=0⟹a=0. Thus, the set is linearly independent.

exm-poly-degree-bound.title: Polynomials of Bounded Degree
exm-poly-degree-bound.html:
Let F[x] be the vector space of all polynomials over a field F. For a fixed n∈N, the set F[x]≤n of polynomials of degree at most n is a subspace of F[x].

  • Zero vector: The zero polynomial has degree −∞, so 0∈F[x]≤n.
  • Addition: If deg⁡p≤n and deg⁡q≤n, then deg⁡(p+q)≤max(deg⁡p,deg⁡q)≤n.
  • Scalar multiplication: If deg⁡p≤n and c∈F, then deg⁡(cp)≤deg⁡p≤n.

exm-poly-exact-degree.title: Polynomials of Exact Degree
exm-poly-exact-degree.html:
The set F[x]=n of polynomials of degree exactly n is not a subspace of F[x].

  • It does not contain the zero vector (since deg⁡0=−∞≠n).
  • It is not closed under addition. For example, if p(x)=xn+x and q(x)=−xn, both have degree n, but p(x)+q(x)=x, which has degree 1≠n (assuming n>1).

exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2.title: \nQ Adjoin \sqrt{2}
exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2.title_html: Q Adjoin 2
exm-q-adjoin-sqrt2.html: Show that Q(2):={a+b2:a,b∈Q} is a vector space over Q by checking all eight axioms.

exm-sifting.title: Sifting Example
exm-sifting.html:
Consider S={v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6} in R3 where: v1=(1,1,1),v2=(2,2,2),v3=(1,0,0),v4=(3,2,2),v5=(1,1,0),v6=(0,0,1).

We apply the sifting method (@thm-sift):

  • v1≠0, so v1 is kept.
  • v2=2v1, so v2 is removed.
  • v3 is not a linear combination of v1, so v3 is kept.
  • v4=2v1+1v3, so v4 is removed.
  • Suppose v5=av1+bv3. Then (1,1,0)=(a+b,a,a), which gives a=0 and a+b=1, so b=1. But then the second coordinate gives 1=a=0, which is a contradiction. So v5 is not a linear combination of v1,v3. Hence, v5 is kept.
  • v6=(0,0,1)=(1,1,1)−(1,1,0)=v1−v5, so v6 is removed.

The sifted set is S′={v1,v3,v5}={(1,1,1),(1,0,0),(1,1,0)}, which is linearly independent and spans the same space as S.

exm-sifting-r2.title: Sifting in \nR^2
exm-sifting-r2.title_html: Sifting in R2
exm-sifting-r2.html:
Consider S={(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} in R2.

  • (1,0)≠0, so (1,0) is kept.
  • (0,1)∉span{(1,0)}, so (0,1) is kept.
  • (1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)∈span{(1,0),(0,1)}, so (1,1) is removed.

The sifted set {(1,0),(0,1)} is linearly independent and still spans R2.

exm-spanning-set.title: Spanning Set for Polynomials
exm-spanning-set.html: The set {1,x,x2} spans R[x]≤2, the space of polynomials of degree at most 2.

exm-standard-bases.title: Standard Bases
exm-standard-bases.html:
Commonly used standard bases for familiar vector spaces are listed below:

  • The standard basis for Fn is {e1,e2,…,en}, where ei has a 1 in the i-th position and 0 elsewhere.
  • The standard basis for F[x]≤n is {1,x,x2,…,xn}.
  • The standard basis for Mm×n(F) is the set of matrices Eij having a 1 at entry (i,j) and 0 elsewhere.

exm-symmetric-matrices.title: Symmetric Matrices
exm-symmetric-matrices.html:
The set of all symmetric matrices in Mn(F), denoted by Sn(F)={A∈Mn(F):A=A⊤}, is a subspace of Mn(F).

  • Zero vector: The zero matrix O is symmetric since O⊤=O, so O∈Sn(F).
  • Addition: If A,B∈Sn(F), then (A+B)⊤=A⊤+B⊤=A+B, so A+B∈Sn(F).
  • Scalar multiplication: If A∈Sn(F) and c∈F, then (cA)⊤=cA⊤=cA, so cA∈Sn(F).

exm-trace-free-matrices.title: Trace-free Matrices
exm-trace-free-matrices.html:
The set of all trace-free matrices in Mn(F), denoted by W={A∈Mn(F):tr(A)=0}, is a subspace of Mn(F).

  • Zero vector: tr(O)=0+0+⋯+0=0, so O∈W.
  • Addition: If A,B∈W, then tr(A+B)=tr(A)+tr(B)=0+0=0, so A+B∈W.
  • Scalar multiplication: If A∈W and c∈F, then tr(cA)=ctr(A)=c(0)=0, so cA∈W.

exm-trivial-subspaces.title: Trivial Subspaces
exm-trivial-subspaces.html:
Given a vector space V, then

  • V is a subspace of V itself;
  • {0} is a subspace of V (also known as the “zero subspace”);
  • ∅ is not a subspace of V.

exm-union-axes.title: Union of Axes
exm-union-axes.html:
Consider the vector space V=R2. Let W1 be the x-axis and W2 be the y-axis: W1={(x,0):x∈R},W2={(0,y):y∈R}. Both W1 and W2 are subspaces of R2. However, their union W1∪W2 is not a subspace because it is not closed under addition.

Indeed, (1,0)∈W1⊆W1∪W2 and (0,1)∈W2⊆W1∪W2, but their sum: (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) is not in W1∪W2 since (1,1) is neither on the x-axis nor the y-axis.

exm-vector-spaces.title: Examples of Vector Spaces
exm-vector-spaces.html:
The following are classic examples of vector spaces:

  1. The standard example: Fn with the usual operations of + and ⋅ is a vector space over F.

  2. Working with polynomials is common too: F[x] with the usual operations of + and ⋅ is a vector space over F.

  3. Let D be any open interval. Let C(D):={f:D→R:f is continuous}. Then C(D) is a vector space over R. The zero vector of this vector space is given by the zero function (x↦0).

  4. Let F be any field and fix n∈N. Then Mn(F) is a vector space over F.

  5. The set V=R>0 of positive real numbers forms a vector space over F=R under the following operations: for x,y∈V and α∈F, define x⊕y:=xy,α⊙x:=xα=eαlog⁡x. Under these operations, the zero vector is 0=1, and the additive inverse of x is x−1.

You can check if addition and scalar multiplication make sense and follow all axioms of vector spaces.

prp-union-subspaces.title: Union of Subspaces
prp-union-subspaces.html: Let W1,W2 be subspaces of V. Then W1∪W2 is a subspace of V if and only if W1⊆W2 or W2⊆W1.

thm-basis-extension.title: Basis Extension Theorem
thm-basis-extension.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and S be a linearly independent subset of V. Then S can be extended into a basis of V.

thm-basis-theorem.title: Basis Theorem
thm-basis-theorem.html: If a vector space V over F has a finite basis, then every basis of V has the same number of vectors.

thm-dim-impl-eq.title: Dimension Implies Equality
thm-dim-impl-eq.html:
Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over F. If

  1. W⊆V;
  2. dimF⁡(W)=dimF⁡(V),

then W=V.

thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.title: Dimension Formula of Subspace Sum
thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space, and let W1, W2 subspaces of V. Then dim⁡(W1+W2)=dim⁡(W1)+dim⁡(W2)−dim⁡(W1∩W2).

thm-intersection-subspaces.title: Intersection of Subspaces
thm-intersection-subspaces.html: Let W1 and W2 be subspaces of a vector space V. Then the intersection W1∩W2 is also a subspace of V.

thm-inverse-unique.title: Additive Inverse is Unique
thm-inverse-unique.html: Let V be a vector space over F. Then for every v∈V, its additive inverse described in (VS4), which is v′, is unique.

thm-left-cancellation.title: Left Cancellation Law
thm-left-cancellation.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let u,v1,v2∈V. If u+v1=u+v2, then v1=v2.

thm-linear-dependence-lemma.title: Linear Dependence Lemma
thm-linear-dependence-lemma.html: {v1,v2,…,vm} is linearly dependent if and only if either v1=0 or for some r, vr is a linear combination of {v1,v2,…,vr−1}.

thm-maximal-indep.title: Maximal Independent Subset is a Basis
thm-maximal-indep.title_html: Maximal Independent Subset is a Basis
thm-maximal-indep.html: Let V be a vector space of dimension n over F. Then any n independent vectors form a basis of V. (We say that “any maximal linearly independent subset forms a basis”).

thm-negation-scalar.title: Negation as Scalar Multiplication
thm-negation-scalar.html: Let V be a vector space over F and v∈V be any vector. Then −v=(−1)⋅v.

thm-negative-scalar-dist.title: Negative Scalar Distribution
thm-negative-scalar-dist.html: Let V be a vector space over F. For any α∈F and v∈V, we have (−α)v=−(αv).

thm-right-cancellation.title: Right Cancellation Law
thm-right-cancellation.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let u,v1,v2∈V. If v1+u=v2+u, then v1=v2.

thm-scalar-zero-vector.title: Scalar Multiplication by Zero Vector
thm-scalar-zero-vector.html: Let V be a vector space over F. For any scalar α∈F, we have α0=0.

thm-sift.title: Sifting Method
thm-sift.html:
Let S={v1,v2,…,vm} be a subset of V. Then there exists a subset S′⊆S such that:

  1. S′ is linearly independent, and
  2. span(S′)=span(S).

thm-size-bounds.title: Size Bounds for Independent and Spanning Sets
thm-size-bounds.title_html: Size Bounds for Independent and Spanning Sets
thm-size-bounds.html:
Let V be a vector space of dimension n over F, and S⊆V be a subset.

  1. If |S|>n, then S cannot be linearly independent.
  2. If |S|<n, then S cannot span V.

thm-span-preservation.title: Span Preservation
thm-span-preservation.html: Let S={v1,…,vm,w}⊆V. If w∈span{v1,…,vm}, then span(S)=span{v1,…,vm}.

thm-span-subspace.title: Spanning Set as Subspace
thm-span-subspace.html: The span of any subset S⊆V is a subspace of V. Moreover, it is the smallest subspace of V containing S.

thm-steinitz.title: Steinitz Exchange/Replacement Theorem
thm-steinitz.html:
Let V be a vector space over F. Suppose:

  • G={v1,v2,…,vn} spans V;
  • L={u1,u2,…,um} is linearly independent.

Then m≤n.

thm-subapce-sum-theorem.title: Sum of Subspaces Theorem
thm-subapce-sum-theorem.html: W1+W2 is a subspace of V. Furthermore, this is the smallest subspace containing both W1 and W2.

thm-subspace-test.title: Subspace Test
thm-subspace-test.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and W⊆V. Then W is a subspace of V if and only if the following are satisfied:

  • W is non-empty;
  • W is closed under addition: w1+w2∈W for all w1,w2∈W;
  • W is closed under scalar multiplication: αw∈W for all α∈F and w∈W.

thm-unique-representation.title: Unique Representation
thm-unique-representation.html: Let B={v1,…,vn} be a basis for V. Then every vector v∈V can be written as a linear combination of elements in B in exactly one way.

thm-zero-product.title: Zero Product Law
thm-zero-product.html: Let V be a vector space over F, v∈V, and α∈F. If αv=0, then either α=0 or v=0.

thm-zero-scalar-mult.title: Zero Scalar Annihilates
thm-zero-scalar-mult.html: Let v∈V for a vector space V over F. Then 0⋅v=0.

thm-zero-unique.title: Zero Vector is Unique
thm-zero-unique.html: Let V be a vector space over F. The zero vector 0∈V is unique.
